RagShortTexts: The death of Grumbates’s son in 359 brought mourning and revenge demands to the coalition.

Variants.Content: Before the siege of Amida in 359, Grumbates’s son was killed by a shot from the defenders. His followers recovered the body and paused for mourning, placing it on a platform for seven days of funeral feasting and lament. After cremation, the remains were collected in a silver urn for return home. The loss brought funeral and revenge demands into coalition affairs.

Warriors fought until night to recover the prince, then joined the mourning. Transfer of body and ashes concerned kinship honor and burial at home; the resources of a royal war camp differed from those of an ordinary village.

Grumbates’s mourning affected his willingness to proceed, and Shapur had to consider his ally’s loss. Funeral observance entered coalition politics; the silver urn and seven-day feast were not a compulsory legal rite for all subjects.
